authors: Juarez-Solano, Alan Hipolito; Rosales-Hernandez, Martha Cecilia; Velazquez-Toledano, Jazziel; Tenorio-Barrera, Ivan; Perez-Osorio, Ivan Nicolas; Rodriguez-Perez, Citlali Ekaterina; Martinez-Coria, Hilda; Escudero-Lourdes, Claudia; Salgado-Delgado, Roberto C; Torres-Ramos, Monica Adriana
abstract: BACKGROUND: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) regulates neurodevelopment, immune responses, and cellular homeostasis. Despite increased availability of endogenous ligands during aging and neurodegeneration, AhR transcriptional activity may decline through mechanisms that remain unclear. We investigated AhR dysfunction and its association with the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p27 in senescent human astrocytes. METHODS AND RESULTS: SVG p12 human astrocytes were exposed to hydrogen peroxide (50 or 100 microM, 30 min) to induce senescence-associated features and evaluated over 72 h. The AhR ligand indole-3-propionic acid (IPA; 200 microM) was administered after oxidative stress. Cellular assays included at least three independent experiments. AhR localization and signaling, p27 association, and senescence-associated phenotypes were evaluated using microscopy, gene expression analysis, protein assays, and molecular docking. Senescence was associated with cytoplasmic redistribution of AhR and reduced expression of its target gene, cytochrome P450 1A1 (CYP1A1). Increased cytoplasmic p27 accumulation coincided with greater AhR colocalization, and co-immunoprecipitation supported their association. Molecular docking suggested that acidic conditions could stabilize the AhR-p27 complex. IPA increased nuclear AhR localization, CYP1A1 expression, and proliferation while reducing senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that p27-associated cytoplasmic retention may impair AhR signaling during astrocyte senescence despite ligand availability. IPA treatment after oxidative stress attenuated the development of senescence-associated features. Modulating AhR localization and its association with p27 may offer a therapeutic avenue for age-related neurological disorders, although causality and therapeutic relevance require further investigation.

title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
authors: Benjamin Iovino; Nash Bulaong; Louis Boahene; William Law; Nathan Hammond; Mark Potts; Rosio Alvarez; Joseph L DeRisi; John Pak; Yang Joon Kim; Loic Alain Royer
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

title: SOX4 suppresses vascular calcification via DNA-binding-independent regulation of the USP10–HNRNPC–WNT5A axis
authors: Junbo Chen; He Cai; Xiaoyu Jin; Yi Li; Yingyi Zhu; Kefan Ma; He Liu; Xiaolong Zhu; Luyang Yu; Cong Qiu
abstract: Background Vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) osteogenic differentiation drives vascular calcification, yet the endogenous mechanisms that restrain this transition remain poorly defined. SOX4 has recently emerged as a regulator of phenotype switching in endothelial and epithelial cells, but whether it governs VSMC fate and vascular calcification is unknown. Methods SOX4 expression was examined in human calcified arteries, in vitamin D3 (VitD3)-treated mouse aortas and in phosphate-treated human aortic smooth muscle cells. Loss- and gain-of-function experiments, an HMG-box-deleted SOX4 mutant, co-immunoprecipitation combined with mass spectrometry, ubiquitination and protein stability assays, RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing and mRNA decay assays were combined with VSMC-specific Sox4 knockout mice and pharmacological WNT5A inhibition. Results SOX4 protein was upregulated in calcified VSMCs and arteries, yet SOX4 loss aggravated and SOX4 overexpression attenuated VSMC osteogenic differentiation. A SOX4 mutant lacking the HMG-box retained anti-calcific activity, placing the function outside DNA binding. SOX4 interacted with HNRNPC and attenuated the HNRNPC–USP10 association, promoting K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of HNRNPC. HNRNPC bound WNT5A mRNA and was required for its stability, so that SOX4 reduced WNT5A expression. VSMC-specific Sox4 deletion aggravated VitD3-induced aortic calcification together with HNRNPC and WNT5A upregulation. Strengthening this braking axis with the WNT5A antagonist BOX5 attenuated VSMC osteogenic differentiation in vitro and vascular calcification in vivo in both genotypes, identifying WNT5A as a pharmacologically accessible node downstream of SOX4 loss. Conclusions SOX4 restrains VSMC osteogenic differentiation through post-transcriptional control of cell fate, defining a SOX4–HNRNPC–WNT5A axis and identifying it as a pharmacologically accessible target for vascular calcification.

title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
authors: Sayal Guirales-Medrano; Colby T. Ford; Daniel Janies
abstract: Protein –ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated. Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein’s amino acid sequence and the ligand’s structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a bench-mark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method. Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

title: Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
authors: Kilian Conde-Frieboes; Carsten Stahlhut
abstract: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor’s ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while high-lighting areas for further refinement.

title: Multimodal conformational landscape and thermodynamics of coupled folding and binding in an intrinsically disordered protein region
authors: Vasily Akulov; Valerio Rizzi; John van Noort; Alireza Mashaghi
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides, as well as flexible protein regions, often bind folded protein partners through coupled folding and binding, but the underlying conformational landscapes and thermodynamics remain challenging to resolve. The large conformational space of the unbound molecule and its interactions with the folded partner make it difficult to identify and efficiently sample the slow collective motions governing association and folding. Here, we use enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics to investigate the coupled binding and folding of the intrinsically disordered region of FCP1 phosphatase upon interaction with the folded transcription factor Rap74, a process that modulates the activity of RNA polymerase II. OneOPES enhanced sampling simulations reveal a multimodal binding landscape comprising native, flipped and disordered-bound states, and identify hydrophobic contacts as early determinants of association followed by progressive helix formation. Circuit topology analysis further elucidates the FCP1 folding mechanism by identifying a characteristic topological transition accompanying helix formation and its stabilisation upon binding. To resolve the thermodynamics of the process, we introduce Divide et impera , a thermodynamic decomposition that separates the free-energy cost of folding from the binding free energy of the folded conformation. This approach reduces the conformational complexity of individual calculations while preserving the thermodynamic connection between unbound and bound states, enabling the calculation of absolute binding free energies in close agreement with experiment. These results establish a framework for connecting conformational heterogeneity, binding mechanisms and thermodynamics in coupled folding and binding of disordered proteins, with potential applications in the rational design and development of peptide therapeutics.

title: Sequence-based models predict TF binding with negligible contributions from motif cooperativity
authors: Mindel V; Barkai N
abstract: How transcription factors (TFs) selectively recognize their genomic targets among numerous sites containing similar DNA motifs remains an open question. Cooperative binding at neighboring motif sites is widely considered a key mechanism of TF specificity, yet its genome-wide contribution remains unclear. Machine learning models can now predict TF binding directly from DNA sequence, providing opportunities to investigate its underlying determinants. Here, we leveraged BPNet models trained on ∼2,000 ENCODE TF binding profiles to systematically assess motif cooperativity. Although detected at individual loci, cooperativity made a negligible contribution to genome-wide binding predictions. Nevertheless, the models captured differences in binding preferences between TFs with similar motif preferences, even within the same cellular environment. These findings highlight the need to critically assess prevailing assumptions and explore alternative mechanisms underlying selective TF binding.

title: The evolution of the HIV-1 integrase through constraints from folding stability and functional interactions
authors: Zoni V; Cabaleiro-Martínez S; Ferreiro D; Arenas M
abstract:
The rapid evolution of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) facilitates the emergence and fixation of drug-resistance mutations (DRMs). Although variants carrying DRMs gain a selective advantage under antiretroviral treatment, these mutations may compromise protein fitness, affecting viral replication efficiency and shaping evolutionary trajectories. Understanding the emergence, fixation, and fitness effects of DRMs is therefore essential for predicting evolutionary outcomes and optimizing therapies. Here, we investigated the evolution of the HIV-1 integrase, a key antiretroviral target, and the influence of common DRMs by analyzing folding stability, DNA substrate binding affinity, and structural properties across integrase variants using long molecular dynamics simulations combined with protein phylogenetic inference. DRMs generally altered protein folding stability and protein-DNA interactions to a marginal extent, due to their number, position, and physicochemical properties. Several DRMs altered catalytic site geometry, including alteration of magnesium coordination within the catalytic triad and modulation of enzymatic activity by changes in flexibility of the 140–149 loop involved in substrate binding, while others had minor effects on DNA binding. Over long evolutionary timescales, temporal fluctuations in folding stability and DNA-binding affinity were observed, potentially driven by alternating diversification and selection regimes at molecular and population levels. We conclude that HIV-1 integrase evolves under marginal stability, allowing structural variation that supports adaptation while preserving essential activity, which should be considered in predictions of structural evolutionary trajectories. Together, integrating biophysical properties with evolutionary modeling provides a robust framework for understanding how structural constraints influence the fixation of adaptive mutations.

Statement

Viral adaptation to antiretroviral therapies is a major health challenge. Understanding how HIV changes over time and develops drug resistance is essential for improving treatment strategies. Here, we studied HIV-1 integrase, an important target of antiretroviral drugs, and found that its drug-resistant variants can tolerate structural changes while maintaining their stability and function. This flexibility may help the virus adapt while preserving essential activity.

title: An apicomplexan-specific foundation model improves prediction of regulatory genomic signals in Plasmodium falciparum
authors: Brown AS; Yang J; Llinás M; Mahony S
abstract: Genomic foundation models learn transferable sequence representations through self-supervision, yet their practical value is contested. In data-rich mammalian genomes, task-specific models trained from scratch can match or exceed pretrained models on many regulatory prediction tasks. Whether self-supervised pretraining provides an advantage in small, data-sparse genomes has not been directly tested. We address this in the compact, 23Mbp, A/T-rich genome of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum . We trained a Genomic Pretrained Network (GPN) via masked-nucleotide reconstruction on 455 genome assemblies spanning 76 apicomplexan species. We then fine-tuned the model to predict a variety of epigenomic features in a held-out chromosome, including transcription factor binding sites, chromatin-accessibility, histone modifications, and 10 chromatin states. Pretraining followed by fine tuning improved prediction of most features, with most of the benefit concentrated on datasets with relatively little labeled data (fewer than 3,000 training examples). In contrast, a human-pretrained model transferred poorly, indicating that phylogenetically relevant pretraining, not foundation-model status alone, drives beneficial performance. Self-supervised pretraining on clade-specific assemblies is thus a practical route to data-efficient regulatory modeling in small genomes where training data is scarce.

title: Complementary DNA-contact and domain-destabilizing mechanisms of PAX9 and MSX1 variants in non-syndromic tooth agenesis: an AlphaFold 3, ThermoMPNN, and AlphaGenome study
authors: Vono FM; Santos VG; de Toledo AN
abstract: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domains of PAX9 and MSX1 cause non-syndromic tooth agenesis, yet most substitutions remain variants of uncertain significance. We investigated the structural mechanisms of 39 pathogenic missense variants in the PAX9 paired domain (n = 32) and MSX1 homeodomain (n = 7) alongside 77 non-coding/splice ClinVar variants. We modelled protein-DNA complexes with AlphaFold 3, estimated folding stability changes (ΔΔG) with ThermoMPNN, and compared pathogenic variants with gnomAD v4 domain variants. AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics and mutant interfaces were insensitive to point mutations. Instead, pathogenic PAX9 variants acted through two complementary mechanisms relative to recurrent population controls: loss of direct DNA contact (< 4 Å; 50% vs 17%; p = 0.0025) or domain destabilization (median ΔΔG 1.17 vs 0.34 kcal/mol; p = 4.6×10 -5 ). Leave-one-out cross-validation selected a stable rule (DNA contact or ΔΔG ≥ 1.5 kcal/mol; apparent sensitivity 84%, specificity 79%) concordant with published DNA-binding assays for five of eight PAX9 mutants; canonical AlphaMissense (> 0.564) showed 8%-21% specificity across both domains. Mechanism did not predict missing teeth, whereas missense variants were milder than null alleles (p = 0.001). AlphaGenome matched SpliceAI and jointly prioritized seven intronic variants.
